verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern firmly supports an active, ordered, prayerful, debt-paying relation to the civil order. Jeremiah 29:7 commands 'seek' (darash, H1875) and 'pray' (palal, H6419) for the 'peace, welfare' (shalom, H7965) of 'the city' (ha-ir, H5892); 1 Timothy 2:1-2 commands 'petition' (deesis, G1162) 'on behalf of' (hyper, G5228) 'kings' (basileon, G0935) toward a quiet 'godly' (eusebes) life; Romans 13:1-7 commands 'to be subject, place under' (hypotassesthai, G5293) to 'governing authorities' (exousiai, G1849) because the ruler is 'God's servant' (theou diakonos, G1249) and 'render, pay back' (apodote, G0591) 'tribute' (phoros, G5411), 'tax, custom' (telos, G5056), 'fear' (phobos, G5401), 'honor' (time, G5092) is owed. What the vocabulary does NOT settle is the SCOPE of engagement. The word 'authority' (exousia, G1849) is broadly polysemic (carrying multiple senses) across 93 verses (Ephesians 6:12 cosmic, 1 Corinthians 7 to 9 personal right, Matthew 28:18 Christ's authority, Revelation 13 beastly power), so its civil-state sense in Romans 13 sits within a wider semantic field that other texts use differently. The word 'servant' (diakonos, G1249) in Romans 13:4 names the ruler, but across its 28 verses it elsewhere names church servants and Christ himself. The word 'citizenship, commonwealth' (politeuma, G4175) in Philippians 3:20 is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament): a single occurrence cannot triangulate whether heavenly citizenship abolishes, relativizes, or merely orders earthly engagement. The verb 'obey' (peitharcheo, G3980) appears in Titus 3:1 (obey rulers) and Acts 5:29 (obey God rather than men), the same verb at both ends of the limit. The canon thus supplies a strongly attested submission-and-payment pattern AND a heavenly-citizenship pattern without lexically ranking them, and it never names voting, advocacy, or public office. Hence disputed in degree.

scripture.reasoning: Two commands, 'seek' (darash) and 'pray' (palal, in the hithpael form which is the Hebrew reflexive or intercessory stem, meaning to intercede), take the 'peace, welfare' (shalom) of 'the city' (ha-ir) as object. The 'because' (ki) clause ties the exiles' welfare to that city's welfare ('because in its peace you will have peace', ki bishlomah yihyeh lakem shalom). The text directs covenant people to the common good of a pagan polity (state, civil community) they did not choose. The means specified are seeking and intercession (prayer on behalf of others), not the broader modern repertoire (range of activities).

Four nouns of petition, 'requests' (deeseis), 'prayers' (proseuchas), 'intercessions' (enteuxeis), 'thanksgivings' (eucharistias), are commanded 'to be made on behalf of all people' (poieisthai hyper panton anthropon). The breadth 'all' (panton) and the preposition 'on behalf of' (hyper) position the believer toward all, including outsiders, as one who intercedes (prays for others) rather than withdraws.

Intercession (prayer for others) is specified 'on behalf of kings and all those in high position' (hyper basileon kai panton ton en hyperoche onton), with a 'so that' (hina) purpose clause that believers may 'lead' (diagomen) a quiet life 'in all godliness and dignity' (en pasei eusebeiai kai semnoteti). The aim is a peaceable civic order conducive to godly living, not seizure of office and not withdrawal. The text commands a posture toward rulers but does not stipulate whether believers themselves hold office.

'Every soul' (pasa psyche) is to be subject ('let him be subject', hypotassestho, present middle/passive imperative, meaning an ongoing command to place oneself under) to the prevailing 'authorities' (exousiai). The grounds: 'for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordered by God' (ou gar estin exousia ei me hypo theou, ai de ousai hypo theou tetagmenai eisin). The verb 'to be subject' (hypotasso) establishes ordered placement-under, not partisan identification, as the baseline relation. The word 'authority' (exousia) here is the civil-political sense, one node of a polysemic (multi-meaning) lemma (dictionary form) whose other 93 attestations span cosmic powers (Ephesians 6:12), personal right (1 Corinthians 9), Christ's authority (Matthew 28:18), and beastly power (Revelation 13).

The 'ruler' (archon) is twice called 'God's servant' (theou diakonos): 'to you for the good' (soi eis to agathon), and 'an avenger for wrath' (ekdikos eis orgen) for the evildoer, bearing the 'sword' (machaira) not 'in vain' (eikei). The lexical assignment of a divinely commissioned, good-promoting function to civil office grants the office positive standing, which underwrites legitimate cooperation with that function. The same lemma (dictionary form) 'servant' (diakonos) elsewhere names church servants (1 Timothy 3:8, Philippians 1:1) and Christ himself (Romans 15:8), so its application here does not collapse the civil and ecclesial (church-related) spheres.

'Render, pay back' (apodote, aorist active imperative, that is, a completed-action command) governs four debts: 'direct tribute' (phoros), 'indirect tax or custom' (telos), 'fear' (phobos), 'honor' (time), each owed 'to all whose due it is' (pasin tas opheilas). The vocabulary of owed dues frames civic obligations as debts to be discharged, active rather than passive, yet still in the register of obligation rather than elective public participation. The verb 'render' (apodidomi) here connects directly to the synoptic (Matthew, Mark, Luke) Caesar saying (Matthew 22:21, Mark 12:17, Luke 20:25), where the same verb commands to render to Caesar what is Caesar's.

'Render Caesar's things to Caesar and God's things to God' (apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari kai ta tou theou to theo). The same command 'render' (apodidomi) as Romans 13:7. The dominical (Lord's own) saying lexically distinguishes spheres without ranking the degree of involvement in either; it sets a dual obligation and a boundary, leaving the scope of either rendering underdetermined (not fully settled by the words).

Believers are 'to be subject to rulers and authorities' (hypotassesthai archais exousiais) and 'to obey' (peitharchein), 'to be ready for every good work' (pros pan ergon agathon). 'Obey' (peitharcheo) here is the same lemma (dictionary form) as Acts 5:29 'we must obey God rather than men' (peitharchein dei theo mallon e anthropois). The single vocabulary item bookends both obedience to rulers and obedience to God over rulers; the lexical limit is internal to the same word.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'My kingdom is not of this world' (he basileia he eme ouk estin ek tou kosmou toutou). Lexically the clause asserts the ORIGIN and CHARACTER of Christ's 'kingdom' (basileia, 'from' (ek) with the 'from-X' genitive form, source), not a prohibition on the citizen acts of his followers. It stands alongside Romans 13 and Jeremiah 29:7 rather than canceling them. It does constrain the church's corporate mission from partisan identity, which supports the second clause of the proposition, but it does not settle the permitted scope of individual engagement.

'For our citizenship is in the heavens' (hemon gar to politeuma en ouranois hyparchei). The word 'citizenship, commonwealth' (politeuma, G4175) is a HAPAX (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament). A single attestation cannot triangulate whether the noun denotes commonwealth, citizenship-status, or seat-of-government, and ancient usage covers all three. The hapax (single occurrence) explains why readers diverge: the same word lexically supports both an abolish-earthly-belonging reading and an order-but-do-not-abolish reading, and the canon does not disambiguate it.

'I appeal to Caesar' (Kaisara epikaloumai). The middle-voice (subject acting in own interest) verb 'appeal' (epikaleo) shows a believer actively invoking the legal and civic machinery of the state for his protection and the advance of his testimony. This narrative datum (data point) weighs toward legitimacy of engagement using civic institutions, but as a single apostolic instance under compulsion it does not by itself establish the broad modern modes named in the proposition, so it informs rather than resolves the dispute.

'We must obey God rather than men' (peitharchein dei theo mallon e anthropois). The verb 'obey' (peitharcheo, G3980) here is the same verb commanded in Titus 3:1 toward rulers. The single lemma (dictionary form) carries both the command to obey civil powers and the limit when obedience to God conflicts; the boundary is internal to the vocabulary itself, not external. This qualifies the scope of submission and shape of engagement, contributing to the verdict of disputed-in-degree.

'Render Caesar's things to Caesar and God's things to God' (apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari kai ta tou theou to theo). The dual 'render' (apodidomi) with simple 'and' (kai) coordination (no purpose-linking 'so that') sets two non-collapsible spheres but does not lexically rank the magnitude of either rendering. It supports legitimate civic obligation and a divinely held boundary, but it leaves the scope of permitted engagement underdetermined (not fully settled by the words), which is the lexical heart of the dispute.

variant_units_examined.note: Manuscript witnesses vary on the order and form of 'have been ordered by God' (hypo theou tetagmenai eisin) and the participle 'those that exist' (ousai). No reading removes the divine ordering or the command 'let him be subject' (hypotassestho); the verdict is robust across attested forms.

variants.note: Anchor verses lie outside the published 3 John ECM (Editio Critica Maior, the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window. Romans 13:1 carries minor Greek manuscript witness variation in the placement and form of 'under' (hypo) and the participle 'those existing' (ousai), but no variant alters the subjection command or the divine ordering. Jeremiah 29:7 is Hebrew and outside ECM (critical edition) scope. 1 Timothy 2:1-2 shows no doctrinally weighty variation for this question.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Romans 13 and 1 Timothy 2 as locating civil rule in a distinct God-ordained sphere where believers may participate as citizens under its ordinary instruments, while the gathered church's commission remains gospel-focused, matching both clauses of the proposition closely. Grounds: 'servant' (diakonos) applied to the ruler (Romans 13:4) signals a sphere with its own divine commission distinct from ecclesial (church-based) 'service' (diakonia).

Treats Jeremiah 29:7 'seek' (darash) the 'peace, welfare' (shalom) and the ruler-as-'God's servant' (diakonos)-for-good language as a positive mandate to pursue civic good actively across all available means including advocacy and public service, reading the texts as warranting more than they explicitly name on the strength of the seek-the-good pattern.

Emphasizes John 18:36 ('not of this world', ouk ek tou kosmou toutou) and Philippians 3:20 ('citizenship', politeuma, in heaven) to limit believers to subjection, intercession (prayer for others), and tax-paying rather than elective participation such as voting or office. Reads the proposition's scope as going beyond what the lemmas (dictionary forms) command; treats civic engagement as permitted but not authorized as a positive Christian practice.

Holds both cities together: the believer renders Caesar's things to Caesar (Matthew 22:21, Romans 13:7 'render', apodote) while citizenship resides in the heavenly city (Philippians 3:20). Participation is legitimate but always penultimate (next-to-last, not final); the church as church does not bind partisan allegiance, while individual believers may act within civic institutions.

hermeneutics.notes: The texts uniformly establish ordered subjection, intercession (prayer for others), the payment of tribute, tax, fear, and honor, and concern for the surrounding city. They do not lexically fix the modern repertoire (range) of engagement, do not name voting or public office, and do not draw a sharp boundary between individual participation and the church's corporate mission. The polysemy (multiple meanings) of 'authority' (exousia) and 'servant' (diakonos) and the hapax (single-occurrence) status of 'citizenship, commonwealth' (politeuma) are the precise lexical sites where defensible frameworks diverge.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine what Scripture's vocabulary says about the believer's relation to civil authority and the public order, including whether participation in civic life is permitted, required, or limited, and whether the gathered church's corporate mission is distinguished from partisan political alignment.
stem_audit.notes: The stem bundles two claims: a permission for individual political engagement framed as neighbor-love, and a restriction on the church's corporate mission. The neighbor-love framing and the gospel-not-partisan clause are interpretive overlays the anchor texts permit but do not directly state. The verdict is derived on the original wording while flagging that the precise degree of engagement is the contested element.

lay_summary: The vocabulary across these passages moves in one consistent direction. In Jeremiah 29:7 the exiles are commanded to 'seek' (darash) and 'pray' (palal, in its intercessory stem, that is, prayer on behalf of others) for the 'peace, welfare' (shalom) of the very city that holds them captive, tying their own welfare to its welfare. In 1 Timothy 2:1-2 four words for petition are commanded for kings and all in high office so believers may lead a quiet and godly life. In Romans 13:1-7 every person is to be 'subject, placed under' (hypotasso) to the 'governing authorities' (exousiai) because the ruler is twice called 'God's servant' (diakonos) for the good, and the closing command is the same verb 'render, pay back' (apodidomi) used in Jesus' Caesar saying: pay back what is owed, 'tribute' (phoros), 'custom' (telos), 'fear' (phobos), 'honor' (time). Together the words establish an active, ordered, prayerful, debt-paying relation to the civil order rather than withdrawal. What the words do not settle is the SCOPE of that engagement, and the lexical reasons for that are specific. The word 'authority' (exousia) is broadly polysemic (carries multiple senses) across more than ninety verses, naming cosmic powers, personal rights, the authority of Christ, and beastly power, not only civil rule, so its Romans 13 sense does not lexically constrain the rest. The word 'servant' (diakonos) applied to a ruler is the same word applied to church servants and to Christ, so it does not collapse civic and church spheres. The noun 'citizenship, commonwealth' (politeuma) in Philippians 3:20, the key term for citizenship in heaven, is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament), which means a single attestation cannot triangulate whether it abolishes, relativizes, or merely orders earthly belonging. The verb 'obey' (peitharcheo) is commanded in Titus 3:1 toward rulers and in Acts 5:29 toward God over rulers, the same word at both ends of the limit. The canon thus supplies a strong civic-obligation pattern and a heavenly-citizenship pattern without ranking them, and it never names voting, advocacy, or public office. The legitimacy of engagement is well grounded; the permitted degree and the precise gospel-not-partisan boundary are not fixed by the words alone, so the lexical pattern is best read as genuinely contested in scope while affirming the underlying obligations.

license_audit.non_redistributable_reason: MACULA-Greek and MACULA-Hebrew were used for syntax and interlinear evidence on Romans 13:7 and Jeremiah 29:7 and resolve to CC-BY-NC-4.0, which forbids commercial redistribution. Their presence makes the aggregate not safe to publish in bulk.
